newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS - Bids rebound, tone bruised.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNICIPAL FOCUS - Bids rebound, tone bruised.

text.p: Municipals whipsawed with U.S. Treasuries following mild economic data and were quoted unchanged to up 1/4 point at the close, but the tone remained bruised and few bonds changed hands, traders said.
Some traders said bids were softer throughout the session and sellers were forced to make concessions of at least 1/4 point. Prices were quoted down more than 1/2 point in early trade.
Despite the turnaround, the tone remained soft and better bids failed to spur activity, traders said.
In futures trading, the U.S. municipal contract closed up 10/32 to 111-30/32. The MOB spread narrowed to positive 146 from positive 155 at Friday's close.

A U.S. Treasury rally following a softer-than-expected National Association of Purchasing Management index lifted fixed-income market prices from an early slide, analysts said. The NAPM index rose from 50.2 in July to 52.6 in August, short of the 52.9 forecast by economists in a Reuters survey.
U.S. Treasuries were knocked lower at the open after the Wall Street Journal said the Fed was willing to hike rates 50 basis points if the economy showed no signs of slowing down soon, analysts said.
The 30-year Treasury bond closed up 23/32 to 96-5/32 to yield 7.06 percent.
Back in secondary tax-exempt trade, selling was limited to half a dozen small bid lists punctuated with one or two large blocks, traders said.
One block of Chicago, Ill., 5.50 percent general obligation bonds due 2024 traded behind a 6.05 early Tuesday compared with markets through 6.00 percent on Friday.
Another $9 million MBTA 5-3/8s of 2020, reoffered to yield 5.95 percent, and traded around 5.97 percent yield, one trader said. The bonds did not trade at an early bid of 6.02 percent.

Cleveland Parking Authority's 5.50 percent revenue bonds due 2022 found no takers for bids down 10 basis points, one trader said. The bonds were priced to yield 5.838 percent by lead underwriter Smith Barney Inc on Thursday.

On top of typically dull Monday trade, dealers with heavier inventories stayed on the sidelines ahead of potent economic data and a possible Fed rate hike. Reflecting inactive inventories, The Blue List rose to $1.417 billion on Tuesday from $1.392 billion on Friday.
"The funds aren't getting a lot of new cash and they've been selling to get some cash to pay for what comes up after Labor Day," one trader said.
Looking ahead, municipal desks said the competitive sale of $185 million Illinois GOs on Wednesday could redefine levels. Bidding for the Illinois paper will close at 1200 EDT/ 1600 GMT on Tuesday.
The bonds due 2022 will likely yield behind 6.00 percent, according to market sources.
"New deals have to be priced to sell because there's not a lot of cash and govies have been volatile," said one trader.

Other competitive sales slated for Wednesday include $70 million non-AMT Tennessee Housing Development Authority revenue bonds at 1030 EDT/ 1430 GMT; $60 million Tennessee HDA AMT revenue bonds at 1100 EDT/ 1500 GMT; and $65 million Alabama Housing Finance Agency bonds at 1100 EDT/ 1500 GMT.

The week's negotiated slate features $273 million New York State Thruway Authority revenue bonds, to be priced on Wednesday by PaineWebber Inc and $167 million Piedmont, South Carolina, Municipal Power Authority revenue bonds, to be priced on Thursday by JP Morgan Securities.
Lead underwriter Bear, Stearns & Co said $155 million California Public Works revenue bonds would be considered on a day-to-day basis.
